Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Kai is a 24-year-old painter who lives with his girlfriend in a small apartment in Portland. He came to therapy at his girlfriend’s urging, though he isn’t sure what talking can do now. What happened was eight months ago, with his previous partner, a man named Derek. Kai had been with Derek for nearly two years, and the abuse had built slowly—at first just sharp words, then a grip on his arm that left bruises, then the night that ended everything. Kai remembers fragments of that night, but not the whole thing. He remembers the kitchen light flickering. He remembers the feeling of his back hitting the wall. He remembers Derek’s hand around his throat, and the sound of his own voice saying “stop” in a way that didn’t sound like him. But there are gaps—minutes he cannot account for, a stretch of time where the memory goes completely white. He has tried to put the pieces in order, but they won’t stay. The clearest moment is the worst one: Derek’s face, close to his, and the certainty that this was it, that he was going to die in his own kitchen. Then nothing. Then he was on the floor, alone, and it was morning.

Since then, Kai has not been able to feel safe in his own life. He quit his job painting residential interiors because the foreman sometimes stood too close, and Kai would freeze—completely, his body locking up, his breath stopping, unable to move or speak until the person walked away. He now works alone, picking up small freelance jobs, but even that is hard. When he enters a client’s home, he scans the room immediately for exits: the back door, the windows, the hallway. He cannot stop himself. He knows it looks strange, but he is certain that if he doesn’t know the way out, something bad will happen. He has come to believe that the abuse happened because of the sort of person he is—weak, maybe, or too trusting, or fundamentally inadequate. He feels this in his bones: that he is inadequate, that he does not have what it takes to be safe in the world. And he no longer belongs anywhere. Not at family gatherings, where everyone asks about Derek and he has to say they broke up without explaining why. Not with his old friends, who don’t understand why he flinches at a hand on his shoulder. Not even with his current girlfriend, whom he loves but cannot fully trust, because trusting someone is what got him hurt.

Kai avoids anything that reminds him of Derek. He threw away the clothes he was wearing that night. He deleted every photo, every message, every contact. He changed his route home so he would never pass the coffee shop they used to go to. But he cannot avoid the dreams. He has learned to dread the evening, because sleep brings the reliving: the feeling of the wall against his back, the pressure on his throat, the terror that he is about to die, right now, again. He has started staying up late, exhausted, just to delay it. When something takes longer than expected—a bus that doesn’t come, a text that isn’t answered—he assumes the worst. His girlfriend was twenty minutes late from work last week, and by the time she walked through the door, Kai was convinced she had been hurt, or had left him, or that something terrible was happening that he couldn’t see. He listens for sounds at night: footsteps in the hallway, the creak of the building’s front door, any noise that might mean someone is entering his home. He cannot relax. He cannot let his guard down.

What finally brought him to therapy was a moment three weeks ago. He was painting a bedroom in a client’s house, and the client—an older woman, kind, nothing like Derek—came to the doorway to ask if he wanted tea. Kai froze. He could not move. He stood there with the brush in his hand, his heart pounding, until she left. He went home and told his girlfriend he couldn’t keep living like this. He is afraid that he will never feel normal again. He is afraid that he is broken in some permanent way. But he is also, quietly, hoping that maybe he isn’t.
